Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: A needles/medical visual trigger is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is clear trauma-related medical treatment, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in threat, memory, appraisals, or strategies. The rest of the profile centers on interpersonal danger and intrusion rather than medical trauma cues, so this trigger appears clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event
issues.explanation: 'Avoid site of the event' is difficult to interpret coherently for ongoing or domestic partner abuse in this profile. If the abuse occurred in shared/home spaces, the profile would usually show corresponding location-specific triggers or avoidance themes; instead the threat items focus on general vigilance and home intrusion, making this item feel insufficiently anchored to the rest of the selected content.

vignette:
Minh is a twenty-four-year-old Vietnamese-American painter who presented for treatment approximately six weeks after leaving a relationship in which he had been physically abused by his male partner over the course of nearly a year. His PCL-5 score of 39 places him in the clinical range for PTSD, and across the intake and first two sessions a coherent and self-reinforcing picture of his difficulties has emerged.

The abuse was not a single incident but a pattern that accelerated in its severity. The episodes Minh describes most vividly tended to begin without clear warning - a delay in a text reply, a meal that wasn't ready - and would escalate into his partner grabbing him, striking him, and on several occasions pinning him against the wall of their shared apartment while he went completely still, unable to move or speak. He remembers the particular quality of light in that apartment: the yellowish overhead bulb in the hallway, the sound of a key in the door. These sensory details did not stay in the past. They followed him out.

Minh's memory of the abuse is fragmented in ways that cause him significant distress. Certain moments are rendered with excruciating clarity - the specific angle of his partner's face, the sensation of pressure on his collarbone - while entire sequences have gone blank, and he cannot reconstruct the order in which things happened. This disordered, incomplete memory means the trauma has never settled into a coherent narrative he can locate in the past. Instead, when something in his environment touches it, he does not remember what happened so much as re-enter it: the room tilts, his body tightens, and he is certain it is happening again. That quality of reliving feeds directly into a pervasive sense of present danger - the fragmented, non-sequential nature of the memory makes it feel unfinished, unresolved, as though the threat it encoded is still ongoing. And because the memory can be activated by almost anything - an unwanted thought surfacing during quiet moments at work, the ordinary uncertainty of not knowing what a sound means, a sense that someone is watching him - Minh lives in a state of near-constant low-grade vigilance that spikes without predictable warning.

The vigilance has become structural. The moment Minh enters any space - the hardware store where he buys supplies, a client's home, a coffee shop - he locates the exits before he does anything else. When a delivery is late or a client doesn't respond promptly, he does not register it as inconvenience; he registers it as evidence that something bad is already unfolding. At night, in the apartment he now shares with his current partner, he lies listening for sounds that might mean someone is entering. This sustained threat monitoring keeps his nervous system primed, which in turn makes the fragmented memories more accessible and more vivid: a hypervigilant brain, scanning for danger, finds the trauma wherever it looks, pulling forward the partial images and physical sensations that confirm what it fears. The elevated threat state also deepens his conviction that he is fundamentally inadequate - that a person with any real worth would not have been in that situation, would have left sooner, would not still be frightened. He has come to believe that the abuse happened because of the sort of person he is, and that belief, once established, makes the world feel more threatening still, because a person who deserves harm can expect to receive it.

These appraisals have quietly narrowed his life. Minh avoids the neighbourhood where his former partner lives, takes different routes to job sites, and has stopped going to a studio collective he once attended. He manages his sleep carefully, avoiding naps and staying up late to push past the hour when the nightmares tend to come. When he feels threatened - a raised voice on a job site, an unexpected knock - he freezes entirely, just as he did against that apartment wall, and afterwards feels humiliated by his own body's response, which confirms to him that he is inadequate. These strategies have not brought relief. The avoidance means he never processes what happened; the sleep manipulation means he is exhausted and his defences lower; the freezing leaves him feeling exposed and ashamed. He no longer feels he belongs in the art community he once loved, nor fully at ease with his current partner, who has noticed the distance and asked questions Minh cannot yet answer.

What finally brought him in was a moment at work - he was painting the interior of a private home and found himself unable to continue when the homeowner left the room and he heard, from somewhere in the house, the sound of a key turning in a lock. He stood motionless for several minutes, brush in hand, heart hammering, utterly certain he was back in that hallway. He wants, more than anything, to stop living inside that apartment. What he fears most is that he never will.
